lines.text: Every marketplace has the same 3 a.m. problem: orders drop, and nobody knows why yet.
Is it a data glitch, a quieter market, or something broken in checkout?
Today a person digs through dashboards, logs and traces to find out, while orders keep failing.
We built an engine that answers that question on its own, and an agent that acts on the answer, safely.
The engine reads the business through read-only ports: telemetry from the services, and data from the order pipeline.
Every question goes through the same seven stages: frame it, audit the inputs, pick only the methods that apply,
fetch the evidence, evaluate, challenge its own assumptions, and publish a report. Every step lands in a ledger.
The engine itself cannot change anything. On top sits an agent: it turns findings into proposals with an honest range,
and it acts only after a person approves, and only inside a sandbox.
This is a real, running shop, with 200 products from a Brazilian marketplace and shoppers simulated from real orders.
Left: the world and what the agent sees. Right: the engine at work, every three hours.
Now, without telling the agent, we break payments: one in four fails.
As traffic picks up, the engine raises an alarm: checkout errors far above budget.
Checkout attempts are normal, 50 against 60. The failures sit in the payment service.
The engine itself may not act; its policy gate says so.
The agent proposes switching the faulty flag off: about 37 more orders today, 23 to 55.
A person approves. The change runs in the shop's flag service and is read back.
Payments recover in the next block.
So the agent found the cause, ruled out a drop in demand, and stated the expected gain before acting.
It fixed it with one approval, and with zero writes to production.
Next: connect it to our own telemetry, with the same guardrails. That step needs your go-ahead.
